case_study_insert.main_stem: Eastmere Activewear Retail (ERS) is a private limited company in the activewear and sports fashion e-commerce sector, employing a workforce of 120. Founded in 2016 by Callum Eastmere, the business sells performance activewear and sports fashion through its online store and operates a hierarchical organisational structure with autocratic leadership. ERS plans to invest $900,000 in a new automated e-commerce distribution centre with computer stock control, financed by a $600,000 bank loan and $300,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $240,000 a year, a variable cost of $9.00 a unit and a selling price of $15.00, and currently produces 96,000 units a year. ERS faces two operational problems: its seam defect rate has risen to 3.6% and labour turnover in the fulfilment centre has reached 14%.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: E-commerce Operations and Quality Report â€” Q3 2025: The activewear line dispatched 26,400 orders with a seam defect rate of 3.6%, up from 2.1% a year ago. Customer complaints rose from 40 to 63 per month. Median delivery time is 2.9 days. A survey of 900 online shoppers found that 59% would pay up to $0.80 more for durable, sustainably made activewear, and 62% check delivery speed before ordering. A skills audit shows 30 of 120 fulfilment staff have not completed induction on the new automated sorter; refresher training costs $85 per employee.

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.00% to 4.75%, increasing borrowing costs for firms with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.4% from $13.00 to $13.83 per hour from April 2026, lifting wage bills across retail and warehousing. (3) Wholesale synthetic fabric costs have risen 9.4% year-on-year, consumer spending on online activewear grew 3.3%, and inflation is running at 6.2%.

questions.question_text: ERS plans to fund part of its $900,000 expansion with a $600,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for ERS of using a $300,000 share issue instead.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A share issue raises $300,000 without interest charges or a fixed repayment date, so unlike the $600,000 bank loan it adds no debt service to ERS's costs. That protects the $6 contribution per unit on 96,000 units and helps fund a new automated e-commerce distribution centre with computer stock control even if activewear and sports fashion e-commerce demand softens.

Point 2: Equity finance also avoids the collateral and repossession risk of a bank loan, so the $900,000 investment is not jeopardised if trading deteriorates. To be a public company, ERS can sell shares to outside investors, widening the capital base beyond retained earnings. The trade-off is some dilution of existing shareholders' control, but for Callum Eastmere's business the absence of compulsory interest and repayment makes the share issue the safer foundation for a hierarchical organisation with 120 staff.

Taken together, the $300,000 funds a new automated e-commerce distribution centre with computer stock control without competing with the $600,000 debt service, leaving the $240,000 of annual fixed costs to be covered by the $6.00 contribution on each of the 96,000 units. In activewear and sports fashion e-commerce, where the 9.4% input-cost rise already pressures margins, avoiding compulsory interest payments gives ERS a materially safer route than increasing its borrowings for a hierarchical organisation with 120 staff.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to Eastmere Activewear Retail and its financing choice.

questions.question_text: ERS is promoting its activewear and sports fashion e-commerce offering. Consider social media advertising, sports influencer sponsorship, or television advertising. Which should ERS choose to promote its activewear range? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Social media advertising: Paid social ads can reach large numbers of fashion and fitness shoppers and can be targeted by interest, with measurable clicks to the online store. However, competition for attention makes clicks costly and much of the audience will not buy activewear, which is wasteful for a $900,000 expansion.

Sports influencer sponsorship: Fitness influencers demonstrate the activewear in use and can reach the 62%% of surveyed shoppers who check delivery and product details before ordering. Credibility and engagement are high, but outcomes depend on the influencer's reputation and can be harder to control.

Television advertising: TV gives unmatched mass reach and can build brand awareness fast, but production and airtime are extremely expensive and poorly targeted for an online-only activewear and sports fashion e-commerce brand with 120 staff.

Recommendation: ERS should choose sports influencer sponsorship. It reaches credible fitness and fashion audiences, demonstrates product durability and supports the premium implied by the survey's 900% figure, at controllable cost. Television is rejected as prohibitively expensive and untargeted, and generic social media advertising is rejected because its clicks are costly and less credible than an influencer demonstrating activewear in use.

With fixed costs of $240,000 a year and a $600,000 loan to service, ERS needs volume at a controlled cost, so the chosen method must reach buyers who will actually convert; that is why the two rejected options, despite their superficial appeal, are set aside in favour of the more targeted approach. The decision should be reviewed against the sales and enquiry figures in Appendix 1 after one campaign cycle, and the spend justified only if the extra orders cover the $6.00 contribution needed toward the $240,000 fixed costs of the activewear and sports fashion e-commerce business.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge of promotional methods with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of the business with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of Eastmere Activewear Retail with a well-justified recommendation explaining why the two rejected options lose.

questions.question_text: ERS's defect rate has risen to 3.6% and labour turnover to 14%. Explain two benefits for ERS of using autocratic leadership in its fulfilment centre.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Autocratic leadership sets firm, uniform standards for packing activewear, directly addressing the seam defect rate that has risen to 3.6%. In a hierarchical fulfilment centre with 120 staff, clear instructions and close inspection stop faulty items reaching customers and help cut complaints that have risen from 40 to 63 a month.

Point 2: With labour turnover at 14%, an autocratic leader can quickly enforce induction on the new automated sorter and reassign staff to keep the 96,000-unit output on schedule. Decisive direction reduces confusion for new joiners. Callum Eastmere must watch morale, since heavy-handed control may worsen turnover, but for rapid quality correction and discipline it fits the activewear and sports fashion e-commerce operation.

These benefits matter because fixed costs of $240,000 mean ERS must keep output close to 96,000 units a year; every experienced worker lost through turnover or absence is replaced at a retraining cost shown in Appendix 1, and a destabilised team would slow the $900,000 rollout. Better motivation therefore protects the quality figures reported in Appendix 1 and the $6.00 contribution on each unit, which is what allows the private limited company to absorb the 9.4% rise in synthetic fabric costs without cutting the 96,000-unit plan.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to Eastmere Activewear Retail's problem, costs and output.

questions.question_text: ERS must train staff to use its new equipment. Consider on-the-job induction on the automated sorter or external refresher training at $85 per employee. Which should ERS choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job induction on the automated sorter: Training on the actual sorter is directly relevant to ERS's operation, costs no course fee, and keeps the 30 staff productive while learning, protecting the 96,000-unit output and the fight against the 3.6% defect rate and 14% labour turnover. Trainers are colleagues whose own work suffers and there is little formal certification.

External refresher training at $85 per employee: A structured course gives consistent, up-to-date skills and a record for all 30 staff, costing 30 Ã— $85 = $2,550, modest against the $900,000 centre. It removes staff from the floor and may be generic, requiring follow-up on the actual sorter.

Decision: ERS should choose on-the-job induction first, with short external refreshers later. On-the-job training is cheaper, machine-specific and protects output while turnover is 14%; full external training is rejected because losing 30 staff from the floor and paying $2,550 would delay the $900,000 distribution centre.

The wider context reinforces this decision. With fixed costs of $240,000 and the $600,000 loan to service, ERS cannot afford the output loss that follows withdrawing the staff concerned from the line for long. The documented problem in Appendix 1 â€” the defect and turnover figures â€” makes early practical competence on the actual equipment more valuable than a generic certificate. A short external top-up later can add formal recognition without the disruption of full off-the-job training, so the chosen blend protects both the 96,000-unit volume and the quality the private limited company is trying to improve as it invests $900,000 in new activewear and sports fashion e-commerce capacity.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to the business.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of the business.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of Eastmere Activewear Retail with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how ERS's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs Ã· Contribution per unit. Substitution: $240,000 Ã· ($15.00 âˆ’ $9.00) = $240,000 Ã· $6.00 = 40,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 40,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price âˆ’ Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $15.00 âˆ’ $9.00 = $6.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $6.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways ERS's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Managers can compare the 40,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 96,000 units, giving a margin of safety of 56,000 units, to judge whether the $900,000 investment is safely profitable.
2. Contribution per unit of $6.00 lets managers model a discount: for example a 5% cut in the $15.00 selling price would lower contribution and show the extra volume needed to cover $240,000 fixed costs.
3. With $240,000 fixed costs and $6.00 contribution, managers can set the sales volumes needed to service the $600,000 loan before committing further capital to a new automated e-commerce distribution centre with computer stock control.
4. Unit cost of about $11.50 ($240,000 Ã· 96,000 units + $9.00) can be benchmarked each quarter to spot waste from the synthetic fabric cost inflation of 9.4% and to check whether the $9.00 variable cost can be renegotiated. Together these figures guide pricing, volume and cost control at ERS.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 40,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $6.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety of 56,000 units against 96,000 output; pricing/discount modelling against $240,000 fixed costs; loan-service volume for the $900,000 expansion; and unit-cost benchmarking at about $11.50 to tackle 9.4% input-cost inflation.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate ERS's liquidity by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has ERS's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.26 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.37 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.54 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.74 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $180 inventories + $95 trade receivables + $40 cash = $315; 2025 current assets = $150 + $120 + $58 = $328. Dividing by current liabilities of $250 (2024) and $240 (2025) gives the 2024 figure of 1.26 and the 2025 figure of 1.37. For the second measure, (current assets âˆ’ inventories) Ã· current liabilities gives 2024: ($315 âˆ’ $180) Ã· $250 = $135 Ã· $250 = 0.54; 2025: ($328 âˆ’ $150) Ã· $240 = $178 Ã· $240 = 0.74.

Evaluation: Liquidity has strengthened on both measures. The 2024 coverage of 1.26 rose to 1.37 in 2025, meaning current assets cover short-term obligations more comfortably, helped by current liabilities falling from $250 to $240. The stricter measure, which excludes inventories, improved from 0.54 to 0.74, so ERS is less dependent on selling stock to meet debts â€” important while it services a $600,000 loan and funds a $900,000 expansion. Trade receivables moved from $95 to $120, tying up cash that could be slower to collect, and inventories moved from $180 to $150, so availability for peak demand should still be watched. Non-current assets grew from $2,100 to $2,650, consistent with the new investment, while capital employed rose from $2,400 to $2,900.

Conclusion: ERS's financial position has improved. Both short-term solvency measures rose (1.26 to 1.37 and 0.54 to 0.74) and the improvement does not rely on inventory alone. The main residual risk is the $120 of trade receivables, so tighter credit control is advisable before further expansion.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether Eastmere Activewear Retail's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for ERS of switching to durable, sustainably made activewear fabric.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Durable, sustainably made fabric supports the premium implied by the 59% of surveyed shoppers willing to pay $62% more, helping ERS protect the $6 contribution per unit and address the 3.6% seam defect problem.

Disadvantage: Sustainable, durable fabric costs more, raising the $9.00 variable cost; with synthetic fabric costs up 9.4% the margin could be squeezed. The 62%% who check delivery speed may still choose faster rivals if ERS's service slips.

Managers should set the premium against the $6.00 contribution per unit and the $240,000 annual fixed costs: the survey evidence in Appendix 1 suggests customers will pay more, but the 9.4% rise in synthetic fabric costs and the need to sustain 96,000 units mean the net gain must be checked. If volumes fall, the extra cost would not be recovered, so the effect should be reviewed after one quarter. For a private limited company with 120 staff, the change also affects training and the brand Callum Eastmere has built, so it belongs alongside the service and quality improvements already reported in Appendix 1 rather than being introduced in isolation.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to Eastmere Activewear Retail's data, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 4.75%, the 6.4% minimum wage increase and the 9.4% rise in synthetic fabric input costs will affect ERS. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.00% to 4.75%): The insert states ERS has a $600,000 bank loan. A rise of 0.75 percentage points adds 0.75% Ã— $600,000 = $4,500 a year if the loan is variable-rate; if the rate is fixed, the direct effect is nil. Higher base rates could also raise the cost of future borrowing for the $900,000 expansion and make consumers more cautious about activewear and sports fashion e-commerce spending.

Minimum wage increase (6.4%, to $13.83 per hour): With a workforce of 120, this raises wage costs in the partly hourly-paid fulfilment and store roles. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay rates, so no defensible annual wage bill can be invented. The only honest yardstick is the productivity already derivable: 96,000 units Ã· 120 staff = 800 units per worker. A wage rise is absorbable only if productivity holds near that level or output grows, otherwise unit labour costs rise and the $6.00 contribution per unit shrinks.

Input cost inflation (9.4% in synthetic fabric): ERS's variable cost is $9.00 a unit and the insert does not decompose it, so the only defensible bound is to apply the full rise: 9.4% Ã— $9.00 = $0.846 a unit, which at 96,000 units is about $81,216 a year (96,000 Ã— $0.846). Even a smaller effect would cut the $6.00 contribution and threaten the $900,000 investment; the $62% premium from the survey can recover only part of it.

Conclusion: The 9.4% rise in synthetic fabric costs will have the greatest impact. It compounds on every one of the 96,000 units sold, directly erodes the $6.00 contribution that justifies the $900,000 expansion, and is only partly offset by the premium. The interest rise is smaller ($4,500 at most, and possibly nil), and the wage impact, though unavoidable, can be managed through the 800-unit productivity the business already achieves.
